comments.text:
In Australia, we have a culture of “Avoid, comply, endure, report later.”

Over time, this has produces a form of collective learned helplessness in our population:

a) Reduced expectation of self-efficacy during threat

b) Increased reliance on external authority for safety

c) Normalisation of victimisation as “unavoidable”


This has manifested as:

a) Compliance during robberies

b) Non-resistance during assaults

c) Delayed or suppressed reporting of crime

d) Offenders know victims cannot legally resist

e) The expected cost of confrontation is low

f) Violence becomes instrumental rather than desperate

g) Offenders feel low fear of interruption

h) Victims are perceived as physically controllable

i) Escape rather than resistance is the expected victim response

j) Courage becomes synonymous with compliance

k) Self-assertion is reinterpreted as antisocial

L) Over time narratives like the following have become the norm:

“Nothing you can do in the moment”

“Don’t escalate”

“Just give them what they want”

“It’s not worth fighting back”


Our institutions focus on making people FEEL safe, rather than taking steps to actually facilitate a higher degree of safety such as taking direct actions against individuals calling for harm, allowing citizens to carry protective tools (firearms, body armour, even pepper spray), and they punish people for defending themselves. 

We can see these mentalities in the recent attack, as there were over 1000 people present as well as law enforcement, yet only 1 person took action. 1/1000,

I think we also need to focus on shifting our own ideologies here to emphasise and institutionally support the idea of taking responsibility for your own safety, rather than the current system where all 'safety' is institutionally centralised and taken away from the individual.
